summary: Shortest lighthouse in Oregon: a brick tower with an iron shell at Tillamook Bay, lit 1 January 1890, automated in 1963, now a state park.

light.focal_note: 217 ft above sea level per the nomination; 223 ft in the 1889 Board notice as the nomination quotes it.

lens.where: Original first-order lens, hand-ground in Paris in 1887 (nomination), still in the lantern room; damaged 2010 and stabilised.

structures.note: 40 ft (12 m) per the nomination; 38 ft per the Oregon Encyclopedia, the Friends and the state park.
Automated replacement light on the bench above the old tower; discontinued 25 June 2014.

staffing.note: Two keepers reassigned after the new beacon went in; 73 years of keepers.

access.note: State park. The lighthouse and gift shop are open 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. daily between Memorial Day and 30 September; in winter the lighthouse is closed and the grounds stay open. Tower tours are limited to five visitors per tour, no reservations.

visit.tours: Tower tours, five visitors at a time, no reservations, in season.

facts.agency: Oregon Parks and Recreation Department (lease from 1968; the Coast Guard owned the site before)

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The nomination gives 40 ft (12 m); the Oregon Encyclopedia, the Friends and the state park give 38 ft (11.6 m), as the station record does. The story reports both.
The Board's notice to mariners, as the nomination quotes it, gives 223 ft above mean sea level; the nomination's own figure is 217 ft.

Three descriptions: the nomination (red flash of two seconds alternating with a 60-second white flash), the Board's 1899 list (fixed white, varied by a red flash every minute), and the Friends (about 30 seconds of fixed white, then a red flash of 5 seconds once a minute). Not resolved.
The nomination and the Friends say the clockwork ran about two and a half hours on one winding; the Oregon Encyclopedia says every four hours.

Richard Seaman (nomination), Richard Leaman (Oregon Encyclopedia), Robert Seaman (Friends). The totals differ: $26,000 for the buildings (nomination, Oregon Encyclopedia) against $33,829 for grading and buildings (Friends).
The nomination credits James S. Polhemus; the Friends credit 'Captain Powell' of the Corps of Engineers with the 1886 survey. The nomination also names C. F. Powell as the plan's draftsman.

The nomination says work on the road began in 1894 but also that a mile and a half was complete by 20 November 1892. The Board's fiscal 1894 report says work was commenced and stopped on 20 November when funds ran out, which points to 1893. The story follows the Board.
The nomination names Anthony W. Miller head keeper; the roster lists him acting principal 1889-1891.
'Thomas Ford' (nomination, 1909) and William P. Ford (roster, principal 1909-1918) are probably one man; the sources do not say so.

The Oregon Encyclopedia says the state parks built a replica of the 1895 workroom after taking the lease in 1968; the nomination and the Friends' history date the reconstruction to 1978. The story gives both.

The nomination calls John H. Mitchell an 'Oregon State Senator'; the bill heading it quotes is for the Senate of the United States. The story says only that Mitchell introduced the bill in the Senate.

notes_for_editor: (1) Roster: 53 lines from the USLHS place record (1889-1963), matched by name and position (0.38 km). Coast Guard lines after 1960 are printed as the archive prints them; the story names no keeper or Coast Guard member whose connection ended after about 1960. (2) Friends' 'Captain Powell' and the nomination's Polhemus disagree on the 1886 surveyor; both are reported. (3) The state park page gives the tower height as 38 ft; the nomination gives 40 ft. (4) The Oregon Encyclopedia dates the state parks' workroom replica to after 1968; the nomination dates reconstruction to 1978. (5) The nomination's wagon-road chronology (1892 progress against 1894 start) is internally inconsistent; the story follows the Board's 1894 report. (6) The 1921 Bulletin OCR garbles 'occurred' ('occlTlTed'); the story paraphrases that line and quotes only the clean words. (7) Not read: the Historic American Buildings Survey and any Oregon State Historic Preservation Office file beyond the nomination; loc.gov is restricted to the newspaper tool. (8) The station record's characteristic 'Fl W 15s' is not supported by any source read here; it is listed, not used in the text. (9) The Daily Astorian's OCR spells the place 'Tanzy' and 'Taiuy' Point; the story gives 'Tansy Point' as the paper's name for it, not confirmed against another source. (10) Tower photographs: none proposed. (11) Fact-check 2026-10-22: the Oregon Encyclopedia puts the workroom replica in the 1968 lease period; the nomination and the Friends date it 1978. Both stated in the story. (12) The Daily Astorian's OCR reads the point 'Tanzy' and 'Taiuy'; the story no longer names the point. (13) The 1921 Bulletin OCR garbles 'occurred'; the quote used is the clean 'record-breaking gale' and 'blowing off the shingles'. (14) Roster lines after 1960 (Gedlick, Duncan, Coast Guard) are printed as the archive prints them; no story text names them.
